questions.question: Which of the following Chola Kings raided the Ganga Valley region?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajendra I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Rajendra I was one of the most prominent rulers of the Chola dynasty who reigned from 1014 to 1044 CE.
 
• He is renowned for his extensive military expeditions and territorial expansions.
 
• Rajendra I successfully conducted a military campaign up to the Ganga Valley, earning the title "Gangaikonda Chola" (the Chola who brought the Ganges).
 
• His conquest of the Ganga Valley was a significant accomplishment, demonstrating the Chola Empire's dominance and military prowess during his reign.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chola Dynasty**

 
 
• The Chola Dynasty was a prominent Tamil dynasty that ruled large parts of South India and Southeast Asia between the 9th and 13th centuries.
 
• The Cholas are known for their contributions to art, architecture, and administration, including the construction of grand temples like the Brihadeeswarar Temple.
 
• Their naval power played a crucial role in establishing trade routes and cultural exchanges with Southeast Asia.
 
 
 
• **Gangaikonda Cholapuram**
 
 
• Rajendra I established a new capital city called Gangaikonda Cholapuram after his victorious campaign in the Ganga Valley.
 
• This city served as a political and cultural center, reflecting the grandeur and achievements of the Chola Empire.
 
 
 
• **Military Achievements**
 
 
• Rajendra I's military expeditions extended beyond the Indian subcontinent, reaching as far as Southeast Asia.
 
• He established Chola dominance over the Srivijaya kingdom in present-day Indonesia and Malaysia, ensuring control over maritime trade routes.
 
 
 
• **Titles and Honors**
 
 
• Rajendra I was bestowed with numerous titles reflecting his military achievements and administrative capabilities, such as "Mummudi Chola" (the Chola with three crowns).
 
• His reign marked a period of prosperity and cultural development in the Chola Empire.

questions.question: In 1991, India met with an economic crisis due to ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**huge debts burden**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1991, India faced a severe economic crisis due to a **huge burden of external debt**.
 
• The crisis was characterized by **large fiscal deficits** and **balance of payments issues**.
 
• India's foreign exchange reserves were **dangerously low**, barely enough to cover two weeks of imports.
 
• This led to the government seeking assistance from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and implementing economic reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Balance of Payments Crisis:**

 
 
• India's balance of payments crisis was due to high imports and low exports, leading to a severe shortage of foreign exchange.
 
• To manage the crisis, India had to pledge gold to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral for a loan.
 
 
 
• **Economic Reforms of 1991:**
 
 
• To combat the crisis, the Indian government introduced major economic reforms to liberalize the economy.
 
• Reforms included the devaluation of the Indian rupee, reduction of import tariffs, and deregulation of markets.
 
 
 
• **International Monetary Fund (IMF):**
 
 
• India sought financial assistance from the IMF, which provided a bailout package to stabilize the economy.
 
• As a part of the IMF conditions, India had to implement structural adjustment programs.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Reforms:**
 
 
• The 1991 economic reforms are credited with transforming India into a more market-oriented economy.
 
• These reforms led to increased foreign investment, higher growth rates, and the expansion of the private sector.

questions.question: The Sangeet Natak Akademi gives fellowships to eminent artists. Radha Sridhar received it for Bharatanatyam which is a dance form of which state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Bharatanatyam is one of the oldest classical dance forms of India, originating from the state of **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• This dance form is known for its fixed upper torso, bent legs, and intricate footwork combined with expressive hand gestures and facial expressions.
 
• Bharatanatyam was traditionally performed in temples as a part of the religious rituals and has a history dating back to over 2,000 years.
 
• It is often referred to as the "fire dance" because of its dynamic and powerful movements, symbolizing the element of fire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Natyashastra**

 
 
• The Natyashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on the performing arts, encompassing theatre, dance, and music.
 
• It was written by the sage Bharata Muni and is considered the fundamental text for understanding classical Indian dance forms.
 
• Bharatanatyam derives its techniques and guidelines from the Natyashastra.
 
 
 
• **Devadasi Tradition**
 
 
• The Devadasi tradition involved dedicating young girls to deities in Hindu temples, where they would perform Bharatanatyam as a form of worship.
 
• This practice was prevalent in South India, particularly in Tamil Nadu, and played a significant role in the preservation of Bharatanatyam.
 
 
 
• **Revival of Bharatanatyam**
 
 
• The dance form saw a major revival in the early 20th century, led by pioneers such as Rukmini Devi Arundale and E. Krishna Iyer.
 
• They redefined Bharatanatyam, transforming it from a temple dance to a respected art form performed on stage.
 
 
 
• **Costume and Makeup**
 
 
• Bharatanatyam dancers wear traditional costumes that include vibrant sarees with gold borders, and elaborate jewelry.
 
• The makeup emphasizes the eyes and facial expressions, enhancing the dancer's ability to convey emotions.

questions.question: ‘Per Drop More Crop’ is the main tag line of which government scheme?

options.text: National Action Plan for Climate Change

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY)** is a national mission aimed at improving farm productivity and ensuring better utilization of resources.
 
• Launched in **2015**, the scheme focuses on providing end-to-end solutions in the irrigation supply chain, from water sources to distribution.
 
• The main objectives include **expanding cultivable area** under assured irrigation, improving **on-farm water use efficiency** to reduce wastage, and enhancing the adoption of precision-irrigation and other water-saving technologies.
 
• The tagline **'Per Drop More Crop'** emphasizes the efficient use of water to maximize agricultural output.
 
• The scheme promotes **micro-irrigation** through subsidies and support, targeting small and marginal farmers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Components of PMKSY**

 
 
• **Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP)**: Focuses on faster completion of ongoing major and medium irrigation projects.
 
• **Har Khet Ko Pani (HKKP)**: Aims to create new water sources and restore traditional ones.
 
• **Per Drop More Crop (PDMC)**: Promotes precision irrigation and other water-saving technologies.
 
• **Watershed Development**: Aims at effective management of runoff water and improved soil and moisture conservation activities.
 
 
 
• **Funding Pattern**: The scheme is funded by both the central and state governments, with a 75:25 share for regular states and 90:10 for the North-Eastern and hilly states.
 
• **Micro-Irrigation Fund (MIF)**: Created with NABARD to facilitate the adoption of micro-irrigation techniques by farmers.
 
• **Impact on Agriculture**: Studies have shown that the implementation of PMKSY has led to increased crop productivity, better water use efficiency, and improved income for farmers.
 
• **Water Conservation**: PMKSY emphasizes the importance of water conservation through techniques such as rainwater harvesting and efficient water distribution systems.

questions.question: ‘India wins Freedom’ is an autobiography written by whom among the following Freedom Fighters?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Abul Kalam Azad**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **India Wins Freedom** is an autobiography written by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, a prominent Indian freedom fighter.
 
• Abul Kalam Azad was a senior leader of the Indian National Congress during the Indian independence movement.
 
• He served as the first Minister of Education in independent India, being appointed on 15 August 1947.
 
• His autobiography provides an insightful account of the events leading up to India’s independence from British rule.
 
• Azad was also a proponent of Hindu-Muslim unity and a strong advocate for the idea of a united India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress**

 
 
• Founded in 1885, the Indian National Congress was the principal leader of the Indian independence movement.
 
• It played a significant role in the negotiations for Indian independence from the British Empire.
 
• Key leaders included Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel, and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad.
 
 
 
• **Hindu-Muslim Unity**
 
 
• Abul Kalam Azad was a staunch advocate for Hindu-Muslim unity in India.
 
• He believed in the coexistence and peaceful relations between the two major communities of India.
 
• His efforts were aimed at preventing the division of India on religious lines.
 
 
 
• **Minister of Education**
 
 
• Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was the first Minister of Education in independent India.
 
• He served in this role from 1947 to 1958.
 
• Azad emphasized the importance of education and laid the foundation for the modern Indian education system.
 
 
 
• **Literary Contributions**
 
 
• In addition to "India Wins Freedom," Azad wrote several other works.
 
• He was also a renowned scholar and a prolific writer in Urdu.
 
• His literary contributions include the translation of the Quran into Urdu and numerous writings on Islamic theology.

questions.question: To which mineral group do galena, chalcopyrite and molybdenite belong?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sulphides**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Galena, chalcopyrite, and molybdenite are all part of the sulphide mineral group** due to their chemical compositions which include sulfur combined with metals.
 
• **Galena (PbS)** is the primary ore of lead and often contains significant amounts of silver.
 
• **Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2)** is the most important copper ore and has a brassy yellow appearance.
 
• **Molybdenite (MoS2)** is the primary source of molybdenum, a metal used in steel alloys for its high melting point and corrosion resistance.
 
• These minerals are typically found in hydrothermal veins, igneous rocks, and metamorphic environments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mineral Groups:**

 
 
• Minerals are categorized into groups based on their chemical composition and structure.
 
• Sulphides are a major mineral group where sulfur is combined with metals.
 
• Other common mineral groups include oxides, halides, phosphates, and carbonates.
 
 
 
• **Hydrothermal Veins:**
 
 
• Hydrothermal veins are formed from hot, mineral-rich water that moves through fractures in rock.
 
• As the water cools, minerals precipitate out of the solution to form veins.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance:**
 
 
• Sulphide minerals are crucial for the extraction of many metals including lead, copper, and molybdenum.
 
• These metals are integral to various industries including electronics, construction, and manufacturing.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Considerations:**
 
 
• Mining and processing of sulphide minerals can lead to environmental concerns such as acid mine drainage.
 
• Proper management and regulations are essential to mitigate environmental impacts.

questions.question: Who presides over the Lok Sabha in absence of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker?

options.text: Person from amongst the members of the panel nominated by the Speaker

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Person from amongst the members of the panel nominated by the Speaker**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In the absence of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, the Lok Sabha sessions are presided over by a member of the panel nominated by the Speaker.
 
• The Speaker nominates a panel of not more than ten members to preside over the House in their absence.
 
• This arrangement ensures the smooth functioning of the Lok Sabha even when the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are not available.
 
• The nominated members from the panel are chosen based on their experience and capability to conduct the proceedings of the House.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Speaker of Lok Sabha:**

 
 
• The Speaker is the presiding officer of the Lok Sabha, the lower house of the Parliament of India.
 
• The Speaker is responsible for maintaining order and decorum in the House and has the authority to decide on points of order and interpretation of the rules of the House.
 
 
 
• **Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha:**
 
 
• The Deputy Speaker assists the Speaker in their duties and presides over the Lok Sabha in the Speaker's absence.
 
• The Deputy Speaker is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha from amongst themselves.
 
 
 
• **Panel of Chairpersons:**
 
 
• The Speaker nominates a panel of not more than ten members to preside over the House in the absence of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
 
• The members of the panel are chosen for their experience and ability to manage the proceedings of the House.
 
 
 
• **Functions of the Presiding Officer:**
 
 
• The presiding officer ensures the orderly conduct of business in the House.
 
• They have the authority to maintain discipline and decorum in the House, decide on points of order, and interpret and apply the rules of the House.

questions.question: Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Deposit Scheme (PMGKDS) was launched in which year by the Government of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2016**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Deposit Scheme (PMGKDS) was launched by the Government of India in **2016**.
 
• The scheme was introduced as part of the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana (PMGKY) to address the issue of black money.
 
• Under PMGKDS, people could deposit undisclosed income by paying a tax, surcharge, and penalty totaling 50% of the undisclosed income.
 
• The scheme allowed declarants to deposit 25% of the undisclosed income in the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Deposit Scheme for four years without earning any interest.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana (PMGKY)**

 
 
• PMGKY was introduced in 2016 as part of the Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 2016.
 
• The scheme aimed to utilize the undisclosed income for the welfare of the poor and marginalized sections of society.
 
• Declarants under PMGKY had to pay a penalty and taxes totaling 49.9% of the undisclosed income.
 
• 25% of the undisclosed income was to be deposited in the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Deposit Scheme for a lock-in period of four years.
 
 
 
• **Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015**
 
 
• This act was introduced to curb black money stashed abroad and to impose tax on undisclosed foreign income and assets.
 
• It provides for separate taxation of undisclosed foreign income and assets.
 
• Stringent penalties and prosecution provisions are included under this act.
 
 
 
• **Income Declaration Scheme (IDS), 2016**
 
 
• The IDS was another initiative to combat black money, allowing people to declare previously undisclosed income.
 
• Under this scheme, declarants were required to pay a total of 45% tax, surcharge, and penalty on the undisclosed income.
 
• It provided immunity from prosecution under the Income Tax Act and the Wealth Tax Act for the declared income.
 
 
 
• **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016**
 
 
• This act was amended to give more teeth to the existing benami transaction law.
 
• It defines a benami transaction and prohibits such transactions.
 
• The act provides for the confiscation of benami properties and imposes stringent penalties and imprisonment for violators.

questions.question: Which of the following High Courts were established in 1866?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Allahabad High Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Allahabad High Court was established in the year **1866**.
 
• It is one of the oldest high courts in India.
 
• The court was initially set up as the High Court of Judicature for the North-Western Provinces at Agra.
 
• In 1869, the seat of the High Court was shifted from Agra to Allahabad.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bombay High Court**

 
 
• Established in 1862, one of the oldest high courts in India.
 
• Serves the states of Maharashtra and Goa, and the Union Territories of Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
 
 
 
• **Calcutta High Court**
 
 
• Also established in 1862, it is the oldest High Court in India.
 
• Serves the state of West Bengal and the Union Territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
 
 
• **Madras High Court**
 
 
• Established in 1862, serving the state of Tamil Nadu and the Union Territory of Puducherry.
 
• One of the three high courts in India established by Letters Patent granted by Queen Victoria.
 
 
 
• **Kerala High Court**
 
 
• Established in 1956, serves the state of Kerala and the Union Territory of Lakshadweep.
 
 
 
• **Gujarat High Court**
 
 
• Established in 1960, following the bifurcation of the state of Bombay into Gujarat and Maharashtra.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of indirect tax?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Customs duty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Customs duty** is a type of indirect tax levied on goods imported into or exported out of a country.
 
• It is imposed by the government to generate revenue and protect domestic industries from foreign competition.
 
• Unlike direct taxes, customs duty is paid indirectly by the consumer as it is included in the price of the goods.
 
• The rate of customs duty varies depending on the type of goods and their value.
 
• Customs duty is administered by the customs authorities at the ports and borders of a country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indirect Taxes**

 
 
• Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services rather than on income or profits.
 
• Examples include Value Added Tax (VAT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), and excise duty.
 
• These taxes are typically passed on to the consumer as part of the purchase price.
 
• Indirect taxes are easier to collect and harder to evade compared to direct taxes.
 
 
 
• **Direct Taxes**
 
 
• Direct taxes are levied directly on an individual's income or wealth.
 
• Examples include individual income tax, corporate income tax, and property tax.
 
• These taxes are paid directly to the government by the individual or entity upon whom they are imposed.
 
• Direct taxes are progressive in nature, meaning higher income earners pay a higher rate of tax.
 
 
 
• **Taxation Objectives**
 
 
• Revenue Generation: To fund government spending on public services and infrastructure.
 
• Redistribution: To reduce economic inequalities by taxing the rich and providing for the poor.
 
• Economic Regulation: To control inflation, stabilize the economy, and encourage or discourage certain behaviors.
 
• Protection: To protect domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs and duties.
 
 
 
• **Customs Authorities**
 
 
• Customs authorities are responsible for enforcing customs laws and regulations.
 
• They ensure that all goods entering or leaving a country comply with customs regulations.
 
• Customs authorities are also involved in preventing smuggling, ensuring the collection of import and export duties, and protecting national security.
 
• They play a critical role in facilitating legitimate international trade while safeguarding the country's economic interests.

__
 
• Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were established in 1975 under the RRB Act, 1976 to provide sufficient banking and credit facility for agriculture and other rural sectors.
 
• The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was established in 1982 to promote sustainable and equitable agriculture and rural development.
 
• The State Bank of India (SBI) was nationalized in 1955, making it the first bank in India to be nationalized under the State Bank of India Act.

• The process of nationalization of banks in India was carried out to ensure a greater reach of banking services to the unbanked sections of the society.
 
• In 1969, 14 major commercial banks were nationalized, followed by 6 more banks in 1980.
 
• Nationalization helped in the expansion of banking services in rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• It ensured that credit was available to priority sectors like agriculture, small-scale industries, and exports.
 
 
 
• **Functions of NABARD**
 
 
• NABARD provides refinance support for building rural infrastructure.
 
• It plays a key role in the development of the rural financial sector by developing financial institutions.
 
• NABARD ensures credit flow to priority sectors like agriculture, cottage, and village industries.
 
• It promotes sustainable and equitable agriculture through innovative initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Objectives of Regional Rural Banks**
 
 
• To provide banking facilities to rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• To carry out government operations like disbursement of wages of MGNREGA workers, distribution of pensions, etc.
 
• To provide financial assistance to small and marginal farmers, agricultural laborers, and rural artisans.
 
• To generate employment opportunities in rural areas.

questions.question: Article 51 of the Indian Constitution says that the state shall endeavour to:

options.text: protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife
protect monuments, places and objects of artistic or historic interest

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**promote international peace and security**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 51 falls under Part IV of the Indian Constitution, which deals with the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• The main aim of Article 51 is to **promote international peace and security**.
 
• It emphasizes the importance of maintaining **just and honorable relations between nations**.
 
• Article 51 also encourages the state to **foster respect for international law** and treaty obligations.
 
• Additionally, it seeks to promote **settlement of international disputes by arbitration**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**

 
 
• These are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government.
 
• They are non-justiciable in nature, which means they are not enforceable by any court.
 
• The DPSPs aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
 
• They are inspired by the Directive Principles given in the Constitution of Ireland.
 
 
 
• **International Peace and Security**
 
 
• International peace and security refer to the absence of war and violence among nations.
 
• It involves diplomatic efforts, peace treaties, and international laws to maintain harmony globally.
 
• Organizations like the United Nations play a pivotal role in ensuring international peace and security.
 
 
 
• **Treaty Obligations**
 
 
• Treaty obligations are commitments made by countries in treaties they sign.
 
• These obligations are binding under international law.
 
• Examples include human rights treaties, trade agreements, and environmental treaties.
 
 
 
• **Arbitration in International Disputes**
 
 
• Arbitration is a method of resolving disputes outside the courts.
 
• It is often used in international disputes to avoid lengthy litigation.
 
• Arbitral awards are generally binding and enforceable in the countries involved.

questions.question: The President of India and the Governor of States enjoy the immunities as mentioned under Article ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 361**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 361** of the Indian Constitution provides immunity to the President of India and the Governors of states.
 
• The President or the Governor is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office.
 
• No criminal proceedings can be initiated against the President or the Governor during their term of office.
 
• They cannot be arrested or imprisoned while holding office.
 
• Only civil proceedings can be instituted against them with two months' notice for acts done in their personal capacity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 360**

 
 
• Deals with the proclamation of financial emergency by the President of India.
 
• Financial emergency can be declared if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened.
 
 
 
• **Article 362**
 
 
• Originally provided for the rights and privileges of the Rulers of Indian States.
 
• This article was omitted by the 26th Amendment Act, 1971.
 
 
 
• **Article 359**
 
 
• Deals with the suspension of the enforcement of rights conferred by Part III during emergencies.
 
• The President can declare the suspension of the right to move any court for the enforcement of fundamental rights during an emergency.

questions.question: The Theosophical Society was started by which of the following social reformers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Annie Besant**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Theosophical Society was co-founded by **Madame H.P. Blavatsky and Colonel H.S. Olcott** in 1875 in New York.
 
• **Annie Besant** became a prominent leader of the Theosophical Society and played a significant role in its activities.
 
• She joined the Theosophical Society in 1889 and later became its president from 1907 to 1933.
 
• Annie Besant was a notable social reformer, women's rights activist, and supporter of Indian self-rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Theosophical Society**

 
 
• The Society's primary objective is to promote universal brotherhood and investigate the hidden mysteries of nature and the divine.
 
• It emphasizes the study of comparative religion, philosophy, and science.

questions.question: In general, what will happen with rainfall as we move from the equator to the poles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rainfall goes on decreasing steadily**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Equatorial regions experience high rainfall due to the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) where warm, moist air rises and causes frequent precipitation.
 
• Tropical regions, slightly away from the equator, still experience significant rainfall but less compared to equatorial regions.
 
• As we move towards the subtropical regions, the descending dry air from the Hadley Cell circulation results in arid conditions and reduced rainfall.
 
• Temperate zones receive moderate rainfall; however, polar regions receive minimal precipitation, primarily in the form of snow.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**

 
 
• A belt of low pressure around the equator where the trade winds from both hemispheres converge.
 
• Characterized by warm, moist air rising and leading to cloud formation and heavy rainfall.
 
 
 
• **Hadley Cell**
 
 
• A large-scale atmospheric circulation pattern in the tropics that transports heat from the equator to the subtropics.
 
• Results in high-pressure zones in subtropical regions, contributing to arid conditions.
 
 
 
• **Precipitation Patterns**
 
 
• Equatorial zones: Heavy and frequent rainfall.
 
• Tropics and subtropics: Varying rainfall with arid zones.
 
• Temperate zones: Moderate rainfall distributed throughout the year.
 
• Polar regions: Low precipitation, mostly as snow.
 
 
 
• **Climate Zones**
 
 
• Equatorial, tropical, subtropical, temperate, and polar zones each exhibit distinct precipitation patterns.
 
• Understanding these zones helps in predicting agricultural and environmental conditions.

questions.question: When a carbon compound is burnt resulting in a clean flame, it indicates that it is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**saturated hydrocarbon compounds**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Saturated hydrocarbons, also known as alkanes, burn with a clean flame, producing carbon dioxide and water.
 
• They have only single bonds between carbon atoms, which allow complete combustion with sufficient oxygen.
 
• Complete combustion occurs when all the carbon and hydrogen in the fuel react with oxygen, leaving no residue.
 
• Common examples of saturated hydrocarbons include methane, ethane, propane, and butane.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Unsaturated Hydrocarbons**

 
 
• These compounds contain double or triple bonds between carbon atoms and include alkenes and alkynes.
 
• Unsaturated hydrocarbons tend to burn with a sooty flame due to incomplete combustion.
 
• Examples include ethylene (ethene) and acetylene (ethyne).
 
 
 
• **Combustion Process**
 
 
• Combustion is a chemical process in which a substance reacts rapidly with oxygen and gives off heat.
 
• Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, while incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide, soot, or other substances.
 
 
 
• **Flame Characteristics**
 
 
• A clean flame typically indicates complete combustion, characterized by a blue color.
 
• A yellow or orange flame indicates incomplete combustion, often due to a lack of sufficient oxygen.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications**
 
 
• Saturated hydrocarbons are commonly used as fuels in domestic and industrial settings due to their clean-burning properties.
 
• Examples include natural gas, propane, and butane, often used in heating, cooking, and energy production.

• These are a collection of more than 30 inscriptions on pillars, boulders, and cave walls made by Emperor Ashoka.

• The inscriptions emphasize non-violence, tolerance of all sects and opinions, and welfare of the people.
 
 
 
• **Brahmi Script:**

• **Kharosthi Script:**

• **Spread of Buddhism:**

• To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India.

• **42nd Amendment Act:**

• It gave primacy to the Directive Principles of State Policy over the Fundamental Rights.
 
• Extended the term of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from 5 to 6 years.
 
 
 
• **Non-Justiciable Nature:**
 
 
• Fundamental duties are moral obligations and are not enforceable by law.

questions.question: Under Article 21 A of the Constitution of India, what is the age for children to be provided with free and compulsory education?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Six to fourteen years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 21 A of the Constitution of India mandates free and compulsory education for children aged **six to fourteen years**.
 
• This provision was added by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002**.
 
• The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 operationalizes the mandate under Article 21 A.
 
• The RTE Act ensures that every child has the right to full-time elementary education of satisfactory and equitable quality in a formal school which satisfies certain essential norms and standards.
 
• It lays down the duties and responsibilities of the government, local authorities, and parents in providing free and compulsory education, and sharing the financial and other responsibilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **86th Amendment Act, 2002**

 
 
• It inserted Article 21 A in the Constitution, making education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• This amendment also altered Article 45, which now directs the state to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
 
• Article 51A(k) was also added, making it a fundamental duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
 
 
 
• **Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009**
 
 
• The RTE Act, 2009, came into effect on April 1, 2010, and it specifies the modalities of the provision of free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• It mandates that private schools reserve 25% of seats for children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups.
 
• The act requires no child to be held back, expelled, or required to pass a board examination until the completion of elementary education.
 
 
 
• **Responsibilities under RTE**
 
 
• The central and state governments share the financial responsibility for implementing the RTE Act.
 
• Local authorities are responsible for ensuring that every child of the age of six to fourteen years is enrolled, attends school, and completes elementary education.
 
• Schools are required to conform to the norms and standards specified in the schedule to the RTE Act.
 
 
 
• **Impact of RTE Act**
 
 
• The RTE Act has significantly increased enrollment rates in elementary education.
 
• It has improved the infrastructure and quality of education in government schools.
 
• However, challenges remain in terms of implementation, quality of education, and teacher accountability.

questions.question: Which of the following is a state where more people are engaged in work than are really needed?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Disguised Unemployment** occurs when more people are employed than are necessary for a given level of output.
 
• It is often observed in the **agricultural sector** where family members work on the same plot of land without a proportional increase in productivity.
 
• In disguised unemployment, the marginal productivity of labor is **zero or negligible**.
 
• It is a common feature in **developing economies** where labor is abundant, but capital is scarce.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Frictional Unemployment**

 
 
• It refers to short-term unemployment that occurs when people are between jobs or are entering the labor market for the first time.
 
• It is usually voluntary and is considered a natural part of the job search process.
 
 
 
• **Open Unemployment**
 
 
• This type of unemployment occurs when individuals who are willing and able to work cannot find jobs.
 
• It is easily observable and measurable through unemployment rates.
 
 
 
• **Seasonal Unemployment**
 
 
• It occurs when people are unemployed at certain times of the year because their work is seasonal.
 
• Examples include agricultural workers during the off-season and workers in the tourism industry during non-peak seasons.

questions.question: Which of the following constitutes a food chain starting from producer to top carnivores?

options.text: Small Plants → Insects → Fish → Birds → Tigers

questions.solution:

• A food chain represents the sequence of organisms through which nutrients and energy pass as one organism eats another.
 
• Producers like grass form the base of the food chain, converting solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.
 
• Primary consumers, such as insects, feed on producers and are then consumed by secondary consumers like snakes.
 
• Tertiary consumers, such as birds, feed on secondary consumers, while top carnivores, like tigers, are at the top of the food chain, preying on other animals.
 
• This food chain exemplifies the flow of energy from producers to top carnivores, maintaining the balance within an ecosystem.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Primary Consumers:** Herbivores that feed on primary producers, such as plants or algae.
 
• **Secondary Consumers:** Carnivores or omnivores that feed on primary consumers.
 
• **Tertiary Consumers:** Predators that feed on secondary consumers and often occupy the top position in a food chain.
 
• **Energy Flow in Ecosystems:** The movement of energy through a series of organisms as each one consumes another, starting with solar energy captured by producers.

• Chidambaram Temple is one of the **Pancha Bhoota Stalas**, representing the element of space (Akasha).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pancha Bhoota Stalas**

 
 
• These are five major Shiva temples, each representing one of the five elements: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Space.
 
• The temples are located in South India and are significant pilgrimage sites for devotees of Lord Shiva.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Equator**
 
 
• The magnetic equator is an imaginary line around the Earth where the magnetic field is horizontal to the Earth's surface.
 
• This line differs from the geographic equator and is significant in geomagnetic studies.
 
 
 
• **Dravidian Architecture**
 
 
• It is a style of temple architecture that emerged in the southern part of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Characterized by pyramid-shaped towers, intricate carvings, and large complexes, it is a hallmark of South Indian culture.
 
 
 
• **Nataraja**
 
 
• Nataraja is a depiction of the Hindu god Shiva as the cosmic dancer who performs the divine dance to destroy a weary universe and make preparations for the gods to create the universe anew.
 
• This form symbolizes the cycle of creation, preservation, and destruction.

questions.question: What is the approximate circumference of a cricket ball?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Around 9 inches**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The standard circumference of a cricket ball is approximately **8.81 to 9 inches** (22.4 to 22.9 cm).
 
• A cricket ball's weight ranges between **5.5 to 5.75 ounces** (155.9 to 163 grams).
 
• The ball is made of a core of cork, which is layered with tightly wound string and covered with a leather case.
 
• Cricket balls are traditionally colored red, but white balls are used in limited overs cricket.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cricket Ball Construction**

 
 
• The core of the cricket ball is generally made of cork, which is tightly wound with string and covered with a leather shell.
 
• The leather case is made of four pieces, stitched together with a prominent seam.
 
 
 
• **Ball Colors**
 
 
• Red balls are used in Test and First-class cricket.
 
• White balls are used in One Day Internationals (ODIs) and Twenty20 (T20) matches.
 
• Pink balls are sometimes used in day-night Test matches for better visibility under floodlights.
 
 
 
• **Ball Maintenance**
 
 
• The condition of the ball can change during the course of a match, affecting its behavior in flight and after bouncing on the pitch.
 
• Bowlers often polish the ball to maintain its smooth surface, which can help in swinging the ball.
 
 
 
• **Regulations**
 
 
• The laws of cricket, governed by the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), specify the dimensions and weight of the cricket ball.
 
• Umpires check the ball regularly to ensure it meets the standards and has not been tampered with.

questions.question: Which of the following industrial plants is supplied water from Bhadravati River?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Plant**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Plant is located in Bhadravati, Karnataka.
 
• This plant is supplied water from the Bhadravati River, which is a crucial water source for the region.
 
• Initially established as the Mysore Iron Works, it was renamed in honor of Sir M. Visvesvaraya.
 
• It is one of the oldest steel plants in India, having been established in the early 20th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bhadravati River**

 
 
• The Bhadravati River is also known as the Bhadra River.
 
• It is a major river in the Indian state of Karnataka.
 
• The river originates in the Western Ghats and flows eastwards, joining the Tunga River to form the Tungabhadra River.
 
• The Bhadravati River supports agriculture and industry in the region.
 
 
 
• **Sir M. Visvesvaraya**
 
 
• Sir Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya was a renowned Indian engineer, scholar, and statesman.
 
• He played a pivotal role in the industrialization of Mysore and the development of the Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Plant.
 
• He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 1955.
 
• His contributions to engineering and public works have left a lasting legacy in India.
 
 
 
• **Steel Industry in India**
 
 
• India is one of the largest producers of steel in the world.
 
• The steel industry is a major contributor to India's economy and infrastructure development.
 
• Key players in the Indian steel industry include Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), Tata Steel, and JSW Steel.
 
• The industry has witnessed significant growth and modernization over the years.

questions.question: R.L.V Ramakrishnan won the Akademi Award for Mohiniyattam in 2021. It is the classical dance form of which of the following States?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mohiniyattam is one of the eight classical dance forms of India.
 
• It originates from the state of Kerala in South India.
 
• Mohiniyattam is known for its graceful, swaying body movements and subtle facial expressions.
 
• The dance form primarily showcases themes from Hindu mythology and is traditionally performed by women.
 
• It combines elements of Bharatanatyam and Kathakali, two other classical dance forms from South India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Costume:**

 
 
• Mohiniyattam dancers wear a traditional white or off-white sari with gold borders.
 
• The costume is complemented by gold jewelry and fresh jasmine flowers in the hair.
 
 
 
• **Music:**
 
 
• The music accompanying Mohiniyattam is in Carnatic style, using traditional instruments such as veena, mridangam, and edakka.
 
• Lyrics are often in Manipravalam, a blend of Sanskrit and Malayalam.
 
 
 
• **History:**
 
 
• Mohiniyattam has its roots in the temples of Kerala where it was performed as a form of devotion.
 
• The dance form was revived and popularized in the 20th century by legendary artists like Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma.
 
 
 
• **Training:**
 
 
• Students of Mohiniyattam undergo rigorous training in both dance techniques and expressions (abhinaya).
 
• They also learn about the theoretical aspects of the dance form, including its history and mythology.

questions.question: Which of the following is the first grand slam of the year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Australian Open**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Australian Open is the first Grand Slam tournament of the tennis calendar year.
 
• It is held annually in Melbourne, Australia, during the last fortnight of January.
 
• The tournament features men's and women's singles, doubles, mixed doubles, and junior championships.
 
• The Australian Open was first held in 1905 and has been played at Melbourne Park since 1988.
 
• The tournament's surface is hardcourt, specifically Plexicushion, which replaced Rebound Ace in 2008.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Grand Slam Tournaments**

 
 
• There are four major Grand Slam tournaments: Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open.
 
• Each tournament is held annually and features the best tennis players from around the world.
 
• Winning all four Grand Slam titles in a single year is known as a "Calendar Grand Slam."
 
• The Grand Slam tournaments are the most prestigious events in the sport of tennis, offering the highest ranking points, prize money, and media attention.
 
 
 
• **Australian Open History**
 
 
• The Australian Open was originally known as the Australasian Championships and later the Australian Championships before becoming the Australian Open in 1969.
 
• It was initially played on grass courts before switching to hardcourt surfaces.
 
• Notable players like Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer, and Serena Williams have multiple Australian Open titles.
 
 
 
• **Melbourne Park**
 
 
• Melbourne Park is the venue for the Australian Open and features state-of-the-art facilities.
 
• The complex includes the Rod Laver Arena, which is the main stadium with a retractable roof.
 
• Melbourne Park also hosts various entertainment and cultural events throughout the year.
 
 
 
• **Tennis Scoring System**
 
 
• A standard tennis match is played in a best-of-three or best-of-five sets format.
 
• A player must win six games to win a set, with a margin of at least two games.
 
• If the score reaches 6-6 in games, a tiebreak is played to determine the set winner.
 
• The first player to win four points in a game, with a margin of two points, wins the game.

questions.question: In which year was India's first post-Independence census conducted?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1951**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first post-Independence census in India was conducted in **1951**.
 
• The 1951 Census was the seventh census to be conducted in India, but the first after gaining independence in 1947.
 
• This census provided critical data about the demographic structure of the newly independent nation.
 
• The 1951 Census was instrumental in forming the basis for planning and policy-making in the nascent years of independent India.
 
• It covered aspects such as population size, literacy rates, and occupational distribution, which were crucial for development strategies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Population Census**

 
 
• A population census is the process of systematically enumerating, collecting, and recording information about the members of a given population.
 
• It typically includes data on demographics, economic activities, education, and housing conditions.
 
• The census is usually conducted every 10 years in most countries.
 
• In India, the Census of India is conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Census Data**
 
 
• Census data is crucial for government planning and policy-making.
 
• It helps in the allocation of resources and development of infrastructure.
 
• The data is used for electoral constituency delimitation.
 
• It provides insights into the socio-economic conditions of the population.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Conducting Census**
 
 
• Ensuring complete coverage and accuracy can be challenging due to the vast and diverse population.
 
• Remote and inaccessible areas pose logistical difficulties.
 
• Ensuring data privacy and security is critical.
 
• There can be issues with data collection due to lack of cooperation or awareness among the population.
 
 
 
• **Technological Advancements in Census**
 
 
• Recent censuses have incorporated technology for data collection and processing.
 
• Use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for mapping and analysis.
 
• Digital data collection methods to improve accuracy and efficiency.
 
• Real-time data monitoring and validation to ensure reliability.

questions.question: The __________ is empowered to direct that an act of parliament does NOT apply to a scheduled area in the state.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Governor of a state in India is empowered to direct that an act of parliament does not apply to a scheduled area in the state.
 
• This power is derived from the Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Governor can make regulations for the peace and good governance of scheduled areas after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council.
 
• The Governor's discretion in this regard is significant for the administration and protection of tribal regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Scheduled Areas:**

 
 
• Scheduled Areas are specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
 
• These areas are typically inhabited by significant tribal populations.
 
• Administration of Scheduled Areas is designed to protect tribal culture and resources.
 
 
 
• **Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• Deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
 
• Empowers the Governor to make regulations for peace and good governance in these areas.
 
• Ensures that tribal interests are safeguarded in these regions.
 
 
 
• **Tribes Advisory Council:**
 
 
• Constituted to advise on matters related to the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes.
 
• Comprises members, the majority of whom are representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in the state legislative assembly.
 
 
 
• **Governor's Role:**
 
 
• Acts as a critical link between the central government and the state government.
 
• Holds discretionary powers in certain matters as specified by the Constitution.

questions.question: Under the Liberalisation Measure, the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act 1969 was repealed by which of the following Acts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Competition Act 2002**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act 1969 was replaced by the **Competition Act 2002** under the Liberalisation Measure.
 
• The **Competition Act 2002** was enacted by the Indian Parliament to promote and sustain competition in markets, protect consumer interests, and ensure freedom of trade.
 
• The **Competition Commission of India (CCI)** was established under the Competition Act 2002 to prevent practices that have an adverse effect on competition.
 
• The Competition Act 2002 aims to curb anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, and regulate combinations (mergers and acquisitions) that may have a significant adverse impact on competition in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act 1969**

 
 
• The MRTP Act aimed to prevent monopolistic and restrictive trade practices that impede fair competition in India.
 
• It was administered by the MRTP Commission, which was replaced by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) under the Competition Act 2002.
 
 
 
• **Competition Commission of India (CCI)**
 
 
• The CCI is a statutory body established under the Competition Act 2002.
 
• Its primary role is to ensure fair competition in the Indian market, prevent anti-competitive practices, and protect consumer interests.
 
• It can investigate anti-competitive practices and impose penalties for violations.
 
 
 
• **Anti-competitive Agreements**
 
 
• These agreements between enterprises can distort competition and are prohibited under the Competition Act 2002.
 
• Examples include price-fixing, bid-rigging, and production limitation agreements.
 
 
 
• **Abuse of Dominant Position**
 
 
• Dominant enterprises must not abuse their market power to harm competition and consumer welfare.
 
• Examples of abuse include predatory pricing, refusal to deal, and unfair trade conditions.

questions.question: According to a new definition of MSMEs 2020, medium enterprise turnover should NOT exceed how much amount?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rs. 250 crore**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The new definition of MSMEs was announced in May 2020 by the Government of India.
 
• For medium enterprises, the turnover threshold was set at a maximum of Rs. 250 crore.
 
• This definition is part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan package to support the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic.
 
• The new criteria also include investment limits, with medium enterprises having an investment limit of up to Rs. 50 crore.
 
• The revised definition aims to provide a clearer and more inclusive classification for MSMEs, enhancing their growth and development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)**

 
 
• MSMEs are categorized based on their investment in plant and machinery or equipment and annual turnover.
 
• They play a crucial role in the Indian economy, contributing significantly to employment and GDP.
 
• The classification helps in availing benefits such as subsidies, tax exemptions, and easier access to credit.
 
 
 
• **Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan**
 
 
• It is a comprehensive economic package aimed at making India self-reliant and resilient.
 
• Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in May 2020, it includes reforms and support for various sectors, including MSMEs.
 
 
 
• **Investment Limits for MSMEs**
 
 
• Micro enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 1 crore and turnover up to Rs. 5 crore.
 
• Small enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 10 crore and turnover up to Rs. 50 crore.
 
• Medium enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 50 crore and turnover up to Rs. 250 crore.
 
 
 
• **Udyam Registration**
 
 
• It is an online process for MSMEs to register and obtain a unique identification number.
 
• The registration is free of cost and simplifies access to various benefits and schemes.
